analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to negotiate Medicare prescription drug prices and imposes rebates on manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Act was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in 2017 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced a bill to let the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiate the prices Medicare pays for prescription drugs, and to penalize drugmakers that refuse to negotiate by excluding their drugs from Medicare and Medicaid coverage. It also required manufacturers to pay rebates tied to drug prices for low-income beneficiaries, with the rebates deposited into the Medicare prescription drug account. The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on October 25, 2017. The committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and no vote was ever taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million older and disabled Americans enrolled in Medicare Part D, who would pay lower out-of-pocket costs if the government negotiated drug prices down and drugmakers were required to pay rebates. The Medicare program itself would save, since the bill directs negotiated prices and manufacturer rebates into the Medicare prescription drug account, which could help hold down premiums and taxpayer costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices for covered Part D drugs and to negotiate at least two drugs in each therapeutic category, using the government's purchasing power to seek lower prices.
Drugmakers that do not enter a rebate agreement could have their drugs excluded from Medicare and Medicaid coverage, a strong penalty meant to force them to negotiate.

Manufacturers would owe rebates tied to prices for low-income beneficiaries, and those rebates would be deposited into the Medicare prescription drug account rather than kept by plans or intermediaries.
The bill adds oversight and reporting requirements so regulators and the public can see pricing information reported by plan sponsors.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose pricing power and owe rebates on drugs sold through Medicare and Medicaid if they refused to negotiate. Medicare prescription drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers would also face new reporting duties and changes to how low-income rebates are passed through.

drawbacks.text: Drugmakers and their allies argued that government negotiation amounts to price controls, and that forcing lower prices could reduce the money available for developing new medicines — an objection supporters would have to weigh against the savings.

The bill made big structural changes to the Part D program, which Medicare plans, pharmacy benefit managers, and drugmakers had built their businesses around, so the transition would have been contested and costly for those intermediaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare enrollees and the federal budget, the gains would likely have been large: lower negotiated prices and mandatory rebates flow directly to seniors and to the Medicare trust fund. The cost falls on pharmaceutical manufacturers' revenue, and possibly on some future drug development. The main honest caveat is that aggressive price-setting can trade off against future innovation; the bill's design tried to address refusal to negotiate with the blunt penalty of coverage exclusion.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Sen. Sanders on October 25, 2017 and read twice, which is the formal first step before a Senate committee referral.
It was referred the same day to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare.
The Finance Committee never held a markup on the bill, the full Senate never debated it, and no roll-call vote was ever taken during the 115th Congress.
The bill drew 7 cosponsors, all senators aligned with the Democratic conference, and no Republican support.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee without any vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept full freedom to set Medicare drug prices without negotiation or mandatory rebates. The Senate Finance Committee majority, which chose not to take the bill up, faced no vote on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drugmakers; no vote was ever held

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 7 cosponsors.

for.name: 7 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding no Republican support.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed government negotiation of Medicare drug prices; their opposition was the principal obstacle to any committee action on such bills in this period.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's supporters were a single senator plus 7 allied cosponsors and no Republicans; with Republicans controlling the Senate and the Finance Committee, the fight lined up on party lines.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped drugmakers of the power to set Medicare prices unilaterally, required negotiated prices across therapeutic categories, and penalized refusal to negotiate by excluding drugs from Medicare and Medicaid. Their interest in killing it ran directly against enrollees' interest in lower prices.

industries.industry: Medicare prescription drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plans would face new reporting requirements and rules ensuring low-income rebates are passed through rather than retained as profits, but they would remain the channel through which Medicare drug coverage is delivered.
